claims.text: Near-equiatomic multi-element alloys can form solid-solution structures.
Conventional physical or chemical fabrication methods produce the nanoparticle initial state addressed by the hypothesis.
The proposed intervention consists of rapid cooling immediately after nanoparticle formation followed by a tailored anneal.
Rapid cooling followed by optimized annealing enhances chemical homogeneity.
Rapid cooling followed by optimized annealing suppresses reactive-element surface segregation.
Enhanced homogeneity and reduced surface segregation improve structural and chemical stability during high-temperature operation.
Rapid cooling minimizes the time available for elemental diffusion and concentration-gradient development.
An optimized anneal can restore uniform phase mixing without significant mobility of reactive elements.
Suppressing segregation limits localized reactive sites that can initiate oxidation.
Suppressing segregation limits localized sites that can initiate phase separation during high-temperature exposure.
Refractory multi-principal-element alloys are candidates for high-temperature applications, with some retaining high strength at or above 1000 °C.
The specified catalytic range of 773–1173 K and thermoelectric range of 473–1923 K are representative service regimes for the proposed nanoparticles.
Rapidly cooled and annealed nanoparticles will show significantly less reactive-element segregation than slower-cooled, unannealed controls after identical service.
Rapidly cooled and annealed nanoparticles will show lower surface oxidation than slower-cooled, unannealed controls.
Rapidly cooled and annealed nanoparticles will show fewer signs of phase separation than slower-cooled, unannealed controls.
Nanoparticles produced by slower cooling without targeted annealing typically exhibit measurable reactive-element segregation and subsequent high-temperature degradation.
Oxidation behavior in refractory high-entropy alloys depends strongly on alloy composition and testing conditions.
The magnitude of improvement from the proposed protocol may vary with alloy composition and exposure duration.
The hypothesis applies primarily where chemical homogeneity governs nanoparticle stability and may fail where other stabilization mechanisms dominate or temperatures exceed the stated ranges.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in segregation, oxidation, or phase separation relative to the slower-cooled control would falsify the hypothesis.
